subject: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data

messages.author: f3e53d88c5f2bedb
messages.subject: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
parts:
To preface, this is my first foray into CFA and SEM, so please forgive me as I am likely making a number of unwitting mistakes.


I am currently working on a study to validate a proposed psychometric attitudinal scale. We have a number of indicator terms obtained from previous literature and from structured interviews (referred to here as x1 ... x21), and an idea of how these terms are related to a few latent factors (y1 ... y3).


Here is the lavaan model of those relationships:


cfa.model = "
    y1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9 + x10 + x11
    y2 =~ x12 + x13 + x14 + x15 + x16
    y3 =~ x17 + x18 + x19 + x20 + x21
"


We currently have a tiny sample of 20 responses and are hoping to move into full data collection in the very near future. However, going into it, we wanted to have an idea--aside from the numerous "rules of thumb" out there (i.e. 10-to-1 participants-to-indicators)--of the sample size required for our analyses. Here is a CSV containing the data, so you have an idea of what I am working with.


Looking into it, it seems like the best approach is CFA with a DWLS or WLSMV estimator, due to the properties of ordinal Likert-type data (Wang & Cunningham 2005, and others). lavaan is unable to converge using either of these estimators on a data set so small, but does "succeed" using ML, for what it's worth. I am not sure if that is of any use.


So, following Beaujean 2014, I went to the simsem package to simulate some data and estimate the minimum sample size from there. I thought that using the distributions of the data we already have would be a good idea. However, when I run the following code, I end up with power estimates of 1.000 for everything aside from the factor-factor estimates, which are exceedingly small (< 0.05).


cfa.sim1 = sim(model=cfa.model, n=rep(c(200, 250, 300, 400, 500), 100),
          lavaanfun="cfa", realData=data, seed=555)
summaryParam(cfa.sim1)


The plotPower() function shows this doesn't change across the varying sample sizes. It wasn't entirely clear to me what simsem was using the realData argument for; whether it uses the distributions of both the indicators and the latent factors according to the model, or just the indicators. I also wasn't clear on why I would be getting 1.000 for all of the power estimates, though I assumed that the small sample size was causing it to fail because there simply wasn't enough information to estimate the distributions. I would be surprised if it were telling me that 200 was a more-than-adequate sample size, considering the number of indicators.


I then thought that, though less ideal, I could give it distributions with a moderate level of skewness (1.5) and kurtosis (3.0) [from Li 2015] and go from there:


cfa.sim.dist = bindDist(p=3, skewness=1.5, kurtosis=3.0)
cfa.sim2 = sim(model=cfa.model, n=rep(c(200, 250, 300, 400, 500), 100),
           lavaanfun="cfa", facDist=cfa.sim.dist, seed=555)
summaryParam(cfa.sim2)


However, this still gives me the same power estimates as before (1.000 for all factor-indicator and indicator-indicator, < 0.05 for factor-factor). Do I also need to provide distributions for the indicators via the indDist argument, or does it generate these from the facDist distributions?


So, these are the questions I am currently faced with:

  1. Is there a way to use the data set I have to estimate the distributions for the simulations and the power analysis, or is it simply too small to be useful?
  2. If not, what is the best way to proceed? It seemed to fail even when provided with parameters for the factor distributions.
  3. You may notice from the data set that there is a 'type' variable as well and that this is, in fact, a within-subjects design (each of the 5 participants rated 4 different samples). How do I incorporate this into my CFA model?
Thank you for any help.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
parts: Looking into it, it seems like the best approach is CFA with a DWLS or WLSMV estimator, due to the properties of ordinal Likert-type data (Wang & Cunningham 2005, and others). lavaan is unable to converge using either of these estimators on a data set so small, but does "succeed" using ML, for what it's worth. I am not sure if that is of any use.

It looks like your items have 7 catgories, in which case MLE sufficiently estimates factor loadings:

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

You can use MLR to correct SEs and test statistics for any non-normality, but the point estimates under ML should not be very attenuated with so many categories.

1. Is there a way to use the data set I have to estimate the distributions for the simulations and the power analysis, or is it simply too small to be useful?

A sample this small isn't going to allow you to have any confidence that parameter estimates will generalize to the population, but there is nothing wrong with using them as population parameters in a power analysis using simsem if you have no theoretical basis for choosing more plausible population values.

2. If not, what is the best way to proceed? It seemed to fail even when provided with parameters for the factor distributions.

I don't see how the power analysis could "fail", so I imagine you are talking about the real data.  You need more data.  Regarding rules of thumb for sample size (N), the number of items/parameters (model size) is not the only issue.  MacCallum et al. (1999) showed that there is an interaction between N, model size, and reliability/communality (how large the factor loadings are).  You can trust the results as long as 2 of those 3 factors are large, but two of those factors are small, the third factor would have to be huge to make up for the lack of information from the other two sources.  So the answer to your question, like so many other circumstances in applied statistics, is "it depends" -- in your case, it depends on how reliable your items are.  Y1 has lots of indicators, but Y2 and Y3 only have 5 each, so you should probably strive for N > 400 in case they are not composed mostly of common-factor variance.

3. You may notice from the data set that there is a 'type' variable as well and that this is, in fact, a within-subjects design (each of the 5 participants rated 4 different samples). How do I incorporate this into my CFA model?

Read about longitudinal CFA and multitrait-multimethod models for ideas about handling dependent measures like this.  Essentially, you can put the data in wide format (the same indicator will be in multiple columns, one for each within-subjects condition).  Then define the each factor separately for each condition (e.g., Factor1_type1, Factor2_type1, Factor1_type2, Factor2_type2) and also define a method factor for each indicator to account for item-specific variance that is constant across conditions.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
parts:
...(1.000 power for nearly all comparisons). Do you have any idea what could be going wrong, or are the results actually accurate (N=200 sufficient for power analysis), or am I misinterpreting the output?

Hard to know if that should be surprising.  By comparisons, I assume you are talking about a likelihood ratio test (chi-squared difference between nested models).  If you put your population values into matrices (like you do for the popParam argument in simsem::bind), you can calculate the population mean vector and covariance matrix using matrix algebra.  Then fit any model to the population moments using the sample.cov and sample.means arguments (setting sample.nobs to any arbitrary value).  Then you can extract the model-implied moments from the model fit, and use simsem::popDiscrepancy() to calculate population-level discrepancy measures (RMSEA, SRMR, and minimum ML fit function) of the model.

M1 <- intercepts + Lambda %*% Alpha
S1 <- Lambda %*% Psi %*% t(Lambda) + Theta
fit0 <- lavaan(model, sample.cov = S1, sample.means = M1, sample.nobs = 200)
M0 <- lavInspect(fit0, "mean.ov")
S0 <- lavInspect(fit0, "cov.ov")
popDiscrepancy(paramM = M1, paramCM = S1, misspecM = M0, misspecCM = S0)

That takes sampling error out of the equation and let's you see a descriptive measure of model misfit.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
